title: Text Summarisation
oneLiner: Make a long text short while keeping what matters, either by highlighting the best sentences or by rewriting in new words, and measure how good the result is.

what.html:
Summarisation turns long text into a short version with the key information. Extractive methods pick the most important sentences and copy them; abstractive methods write a new summary in their own words. Summaries can cover one or many documents, and be general or answer a specific question.

Everyday versionA highlighter versus a pen: highlight the best sentences in the book, or close the book and write the gist yourself.

why.html:
• Nobody has time to read everything: emails, reports, meeting transcripts.
  • Search snippets, news digests and meeting notes all rely on it.
  • It ties together word weighting, graphs, attention models and evaluation.

how.title: Where it's used
how.html: Answer boxes in search, action items from long chats, five-minute news digests, plain-language versions of legal text.

how.title: Three choices
how.html: Copy or rewrite? One document or many? Summarise everything or only what answers a question? For news, just taking the first sentence is a surprisingly good baseline.

how.title: Select, order, polish
how.html: Extractive summaries pick sentences, arrange them sensibly, then tidy them up. Because they copy, they don't invent facts.

how.title: Important words, important sentences
how.html: Words frequent in this document but rare elsewhere (Mars, rover, crater) are important; sentences full of them get picked. The off-topic bakery sentence doesn't.

how.title: The most agreed-with sentence
how.html: Connect sentences that share words; the one most others connect to is central, like the person everyone agrees with at a party.

how.title: No repeats
how.html: Two top sentences saying the same thing waste space. MMR balances relevance against similarity to what's already chosen, so the second pick adds something new.

how.title: A sensible order
how.html: Put sentences in time order for news, keep related sentences together, or follow a template (for a biography: dates, nationality, education, fame).

how.title: Tidy the sentences
how.html: Cut "…, international observers said Tuesday" and replace an unclear "He" with the person's name.

how.title: Writing new summaries
how.html: Neural models read the whole document and write a summary word by word, glancing back at relevant input words. Fluent, but they can state things the source never said.

how.title: Scoring a summary
how.html: ROUGE counts how many of the human summaries' word pairs the system used: 12 of 29 ≈ 0.41 for the water-spinach example. It rewards shared words, not shared meaning.

demo.html: Compare a highlighter summary, a pen summary, and a pen summary that slipped in a false fact.

example.html:
MMR by hand. With λ = 0.5, S1 goes first (0.5 × 0.90 = 0.45). For the second slot, S2 is relevant (0.88) but almost a copy of S1 (similarity 0.85): 0.44 − 0.425 = 0.015. S3 is less relevant (0.70) but different (0.35): 0.35 − 0.175 = 0.175, so S3 wins.

Supplementary Always compare summarisers at the same length: a longer summary automatically matches more of the reference words.

misunderstandings: They copy source sentences (though they can mislead by omission).
The top-scoring sentences make the best summary.
They may repeat each other; use MMR.
A high ROUGE score means a correct summary.
It measures word overlap, not truth.
takeaways: Selection by TF-IDF salience or LexRank centrality; MMR removes redundancy.
Abstractive: seq2seq with attention / Transformers; watch for hallucinations.
ROUGE-N: n-gram recall vs references (water spinach 12/29 ≈ 0.41).
thirty: Summarisation shortens text while keeping key information (TL;DR; snippets, action items, digests, accessibility). Dimensions: extractive (highlighter) vs abstractive (pen); single vs multi-document (lead baseline strong for news; MDS handles redundancy/contradictions); generic vs query-focused. Extractive pipeline: content selection → information ordering → sentence realisation; immune to invented facts. Selection: Luhn frequency / TF-IDF weight(w) = TF × IDF (Mars, rover, crater win); LexRank: cosine graph + PageRank centrality; MMR = argmax λ·Sim(s, Q) − (1 − λ)·max Sim(s, chosen) (Rowling: S1 then S3, not near-duplicate S2). Ordering: chronological, coherence, templates (biography dates → nationality → education → fame). Realisation: prune attribution/appositives; resolve pronouns (He → Gen. Augusto Pinochet). Abstractive: seq2seq + attention, Transformers; ARTICLE <EOS> SUMMARY <EOS> with loss on summary only; risk of hallucination. ROUGE-N = matched reference n-grams / total reference n-grams: water spinach ROUGE-2 = 12/29 ≈ 0.41; rewards wording, not meaning.

check.q: A summary made only of copied source sentences is…

opts: Most central in a similarity graph
